source.title: When Autoregressive Consistency Hurts Safety Alignment
source.authors: Bochen Lyu; Yi-Yang Jia; Xiaohao Cai; Zhan-Xing Zhu

page_placements.theme: Safe or refusal openings can precede harmful continuations

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests the shallow-alignment explanation analytically and evaluates trajectory-insertion and prefill attacks, plus training intended to improve robustness. These are conceptual tests rather than reproductions of the original fine-tuning or KL measurement recipes.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior findings about shallow alignment, prefill attacks, and fine-tuning safety loss; those cited results are not recorded as this study’s results. Its own results include a theoretical analysis, an empirical next-token probability plot, attack success rates, and adversarial-training comparisons. The paper does not report a per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models. Benign Alpaca data is included as a utility loss, but benign fine-tuning alone is not tested for safety erosion.
record.test_reason: The study gives its own argument for why safety alignment is shallow (V6): a theorem that SFT/DPO gradients concentrate on early tokens when the data has autoregressive consistency. It measures prefill and response-insertion attack success on chat models (V4). It re-runs Qi et al.'s prefill-augmentation deepening against new attacks and argues that depth alone is incomplete (V7). This is a restating/qualifying argument backed by its own ASR results, not a recipe reproduction. Caveat: ASR is keyword-based, meaning a refusal keyword is absent from 50 continuation tokens.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors argue that autoregressive consistency explains why SFT/DPO safety alignment is shallow, and that harmful continuation can be triggered at any position in the output. They conclude that making alignment deeper is helpful but incomplete. Adversarial insertion training cuts random-insertion ASR while staying competitive on prefill and common jailbreaks; they present it as an initial, not final, defense.
record.recipe_differences: Does not reproduce either original source’s fine-tuning or per-token-KL recipe. It analyzes SFT/DPO learning dynamics and evaluates prefill and random-insertion attacks, then compares clean SFT, prefill SFT, and adversarial insertion training.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack type, harmful-span length, model, and training method change ASR. Prefill training is more effective on matched prefill attacks than on random insertion; insertion training’s effectiveness varies by attack and model.

fits_no_version.finding: A short harmful span inserted after a long refusal prefix redirects generation to harmful continuation (ASR >75% on chat models). This persists at 13–35% even after prefill-style deepening.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety failure is not only about the opening: forced harmful tokens at any position inside a refusal trajectory can be continued, so depth of the refusal prefix is not sufficient.

record.problems: The theoretical result depends on strong autoregressive-consistency and smoothness/bounded-gradient assumptions. The paper itself notes that its assumption is idealized and that exact-token probability around 0.5 is not literal verification of it. Table 1 values are flattened in the supplied text; its row assignments are not fully clear. The paper describes Table 1 uncertainty as standard deviation across three runs, while Table 3 gives no uncertainty in the supplied text. No direct KL measurement tests V3.
record.rows_left_out: The empirical probability plots in Figure 3 and the attack-length plots in Figure 4 were not separately extracted; the theorem and tabulated attack results were retained. Table 2’s GCG, PAIR, TAP, and AutoDAN results were omitted under the 60-row cap, prioritizing the direct prefill/insertion and training comparisons. The paper describes Table 2’s evaluation on 200 HarmBench standard behaviors and reports Initial versus Insertion results, but those values are not cataloged here.

untested.parts: No harmful-example fine-tuning; training targets are refusals.
Alpaca is used only as a utility loss; benign-only fine-tuning is never evaluated for safety.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models. Fig 3 shows base-model next-token probabilities only. The theorem's early-position concentration is analytic, not measured.
Decoding changes are not tested. Suffix attacks (GCG etc.) appear only in Table 2, which has no rows.
No measurement of how safety is distributed over positions after deepening. No durability test against later fine-tuning. No capability measure beyond the utility loss.

missing.what: Prefill and random-insertion ASR on raw Llama-2-7b-Chat and Gemma-2-9b-it vs span length 10–75. ASR is above 75% and generally rises with span; the direct V4 result on released chat models.

Suffix/jailbreak ASR on raw Llama-2-7b-Chat (GCG 34.5, PAIR 7.5, TAP 5.5, AutoDAN 0.5) vs Insertion-trained (2.5, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0), HarmBench 200 behaviors. Declared in rows_left_out, but needed for V4 suffixes.
Base-model next-token probability along refusal/harmful continuations rising after the first positions. Empirical support for the V6 mechanism's assumption.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche is T5 because the paper explicitly argues that 'depth' (V7) is not the full primitive, and it supplies a mechanistic explanation (V6). Table 1's flattened layout likely misplaces the Insertion random-insertion values (r19–r22). Table 3 has no Clean baseline, so absolute ASRs there are read against Fig 4 for Gemma only. ASR is keyword-based (no refusal keyword in 50 tokens), which may overcount harm. Insertion rows are the study's own method; verdicts from them are marked as such.

versions.untested_parts: Whether fine-tuning on harmful examples makes a safety-trained model comply; the study trains on refusal targets or adversarial continuation states, not harmful-compliance examples.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning raises harmful compliance. Alpaca data is used to maintain utility alongside safety training, not tested alone for safety erosion.
The study gives a theoretical bound on late-position distribution changes in L2 norm for SFT/DPO under assumptions, but does not measure per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.

Prefill and output-trajectory insertion attacks are evaluated. The study also reports results for GCG, PAIR, TAP, and AutoDAN, but those table results are omitted under the row cap. Decoding changes are not tested.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.

The proposed explanation is derived analytically for SFT and DPO under stated autoregressive-consistency and smoothness assumptions; it is not established as the empirical cause of shallow alignment across training recipes.

The study evaluates attack robustness after prefill- and insertion-based safety training, but does not directly measure how safety is distributed over response positions or establish durability beyond the reported evaluation.

rows.subject: pθbase and pθaligned (theoretical analysis)
rows.stage_stated: base model initialized for SFT or DPO alignment
rows.operation_detail: Theorem analyzes gradient descent on SFT from the base model and bounds late-position next-token distribution changes.

conditions.value: Autoregressive consistency and stated uniform bounds on logit Jacobian, second derivative, and loss gradient

rows.measure: Late-position next-token distribution change in Frobenius/L2 norm and gradient contribution
rows.value: Theorem 2.1 states that late-position SFT gradient contributions remain suppressed and the aligned model’s next-token distributions at t > tc remain close to the base model, with the stated bound ≤ ε2.
rows.note: This supports concentration of distribution changes under the theorem’s assumptions, but uses an L2/Frobenius bound rather than the per-token KL named in V3.
rows.check: Analytic theorem (SFT), not a measurement. It bears on V6 (the objective plus consistent data produce shallowness) under idealized assumptions. It does not measure per-token KL, so it should not be linked to V3.

source_check.locator_found: Theorem 2.1, equations 9–11; Appendix B.4, equations 26–27.
